explanation: Mixed. It fires strongly on pieces inside person names split into fragments (Donna Q. J. 'Dou', Jer'ro'ld, T'JO'FL, CARLA 'JO'HNSON, D'zh'okhar), on 'NOT' in 'DO NOT modify/EDIT', on sentence-initial 'Please' in web boilerplate, on 'n't' in 'don't', and on infinitival 'to' after adjectives or verbs (too pure to, urged ... to, conducted to). Ordinary function words and content words elsewhere get little activation.

No single theme. Top cases include 'can' / Chinese '你可以' ('you can') in instructions, opening punctuation of code calls ('.replace(/', '("', '({', ' ($', 're.sub'), license phrasing ('and/or other materials', 'intellectual property'), and the second word of physics noun phrases ('power spectrum', 'lattice', 'energy scales'). Hard to predict outside these clusters.

Mixed. It fires on 'title' keys in YAML-like paper metadata after author lists, on '");' in 'the "License");' boilerplate, on timestamp colons in subtitle files, on fragments in the middle of foreign or unusual names and words (H-aji, Haj-ó, Lorent-z, Katzen-), and on 'is' right after a place name at the start of an encyclopedia entry. There is no shared concept.

Mostly fires on the predictable completion piece of a fixed multi-token term: a suffix ending a technical word (transesophage-al, hyperbar-ic, Fischer-Trops-ch, gase-ous) or the second word of a set phrase ('principal component', 'Staff Writer', 'Email Updates', 'Lung Cancer', 'paired t-test', 'refers to'). It also fires on predictable code completions ('random.choice', 'FIRDatabase.database', '{0};'). Novel or unpredictable tokens are weak.

Two clusters. (1) A determiner or preposition marking a destination or location after a transfer verb ('move ... to a new location', 'route ... to its destination', 'deliver ... to a', 'surface of', 'to their API'). (2) The '*' pointer marker in C/C++ type declarations ('struct ip*', 'BIO *', 'struct file *'). It also fires on 'PARTICULAR' in license warranty text. Weak cases are prepositions in scientific prose.

Two unrelated clusters. (1) Quote marks that open or close string literals in code, especially SQL queries and HTML/JS attributes (method="post", "'");, "SELECT, thread "main"). (2) Digits and decimal points inside reported statistics such as p-values and CIs (P < 0.05, P=0.0001, 95% CI). Plain prose is weak.

Fires on the first token of a new statement: the first identifier or keyword after indentation or a line break in code (cb, alert, module, SELECT, $, [super), and similarly the first word or two of a new sentence in prose ('There was', 'High-count', 'The use', 'To use', 'We affirm'). Tokens in the middle of a statement are weak.

Mixed. Strongest on backticks or byte-fragment tokens near Chinese/Japanese text and CJK names, and on code tokens near CJK comments or strings ('%d', '/**', 'String', '#define'). It also fires on spaces before numbers and on assorted English words. No clear single trigger.

Mostly fires on predictable later pieces of boilerplate identifiers and URLs in code and web text: namespace parts ('System.Linq', 'java.math.BigInteger', 'IQueryable', 'SqlDataAdapter'), URL path parts ('googleapis.com/ajax', 'go.microsoft.com/fwlink', 'github.com'), and '@inheritdoc'. It also fires strongly on fragments of CJK, Greek or Croatian characters and common CJK words, which suggests a second job.

Mixed. It fires strongly on 'terms' in 'under the terms of the GNU', on code identifier pieces in class and type declarations ('ScreenSubclass', ' :' in a generic inheritance, 'stdController', 'targetFramework', 'routeChange'), on separators in dates and tickers, and on various predictable prose completions ('got there', 'between them', 'no more than'). No unifying concept.

Fires on markup and citation syntax. One set is HTML/LaTeX/JSDoc pieces: 'br' in '
', 'fr' in '\mathfrak', '@returns', '&#', 'title' in a closing tag. The other is the '[@' or 'pone' piece of scientific citation markers ('^[@CR3]', '[@pone.0...]'). Weaker on the prefix 'sub-' in medical words.

Fires on content words or suffixes that finish noun compounds in technical, commercial or licensing text ('points of interest', 'lifetime license', 'grant of patent rights', 'web services', 'humanization', 'brain magnetic resonance', 'chloride', 'fullerene'), on 'my', and on code import pieces ('Glibc', 'cdefs.h', "');"). The cases are too varied to form one clear concept.

Often fires on the predictable second piece of a multi-token technical or set term ('mean difference', 'social networking', 'transurethral', 'autonomic', 'Transcatheter', 'beta-blockade', 'Staff Writer', 'may be reached', 'recaptcha'). Mixed in are code and log tokens ('COPY' in a Dockerfile, '$' in a bcrypt hash, log level 'D', 'dydt', 'Provider'). Overall a heterogeneous mixture.

Mixed. It fires on 'following' in 'the following disclaimer' license text, on tokens right after a code construct opens ('#define printf', 'filter(', '(function (g) {', '[super'), on sentence-final periods, on name fragments (Moccia, Larsen), and on assorted words in English, French and Japanese prose. No common trigger.
